tour.title: Asakusa & the Sumida: Senso-ji to Skytree
tour.summary: Tokyo's oldest temple, a 17th-century souvenir street, the river that fed a million-person city, a golden flame nobody will admit looks like what it looks like, and the tallest tower in the world.
tour.overviewText:
Two minutes from the subway you are standing under a paper lantern the weight of a small car, and everything behind it is older than the name Tokyo. This is Asakusa, the old downtown — locals call this kind of district shitamachi, literally "low city", the flat land by the river where merchants, artisans and entertainers lived while the shogun's castle sat on its hill. For two and a half centuries this was Edo, seat of the Tokugawa shoguns and, by the early 1700s, probably the largest city on earth at around a million people. In 1868 the emperor moved here from Kyoto and the city was renamed Tokyo, "eastern capital"; Asakusa kept its own character — temple town, pleasure quarter, and after 1945, survivor.

Senso-ji, the temple at the centre of the walk, is the reason the district exists. The legend is that in 628 two fishermen pulled a small golden statue of Kannon, the Buddhist bodhisattva of compassion — a being who has put off its own final enlightenment in order to help everyone else — out of the Sumida River. The brothers threw it back; it kept coming back in their nets; the headman of the village enshrined it in his house; and in 645 a monk built a hall for it. That hall's successor is still here, and so is the statue, hidden inside the main hall and shown to no one. Around thirty million people come each year, which makes this one of the most visited religious sites anywhere on earth.

Two faiths share the ground, and it helps to know how. Senso-ji is Buddhist. Asakusa Shrine beside it is Shinto, and its three deities are the very men of the founding legend. Until 1868 the two were a single institution; the Meiji government separated them by decree, and this walk crosses that seam twice.

Keep three facts in mind as you go. Almost nothing you see is old: the great halls and gates are concrete reconstructions from the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, because the firebombing of 10 March 1945 burned this quarter flat — around 100,000 people died that night, by most estimates, and the temple lost buildings that had been national treasures. Second, this is a working neighbourhood, not a film set: people live above the shops and pray here before work. Third, money is the Japanese yen, written ¥; the temple and the shrine are free, the tower at the end is not.

The walk is short and almost entirely flat — roughly three kilometres, north through the temple down to the river, then across the water to the tower — and it works as one slow half-day, or better, as a morning and an evening with a rest in between. Start at first light: the temple hall opens at 06:00, or 06:30 from October to March, and for an hour it belongs to nobody but the pigeons and a few shopkeepers. February here is cold, dry and often startlingly clear, and it is the best month of the year to see Mount Fuji from a tower. Be back on the bridge at dusk.

Eat a fried sweet bean bun, do not clap at the temple, and save the tallest tower in the world for the dark.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Flat, paved and step-free almost the whole way, with one long stretch of riverside promenade and one bridge crossing. It is short in distance but heavy in standing: the temple courtyard, the shrine, the park and the tower all invite you to stop, and the tower queues add time. The only real effort is the crowd on Nakamise after 10:00.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Split it. Start at first light, around 06:30 to 07:00, when the temple hall is open, the incense is lit and Nakamise is empty behind its painted shutters. Walk the full route, then eat and rest. Come back over the Azuma Bridge in the late afternoon and go up the Skytree for the last hour of daylight and the first of dark — February gives the clearest air of the year and the best chance of Mount Fuji. Temple and shrine are free and open at all hours, but the tower's last admission is roughly an hour before closing.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: Kaminarimon Gate (Thunder Gate)
stops.narration:
Everything in Asakusa begins at this gate, and the gate begins with the lantern. It is 3.9 metres tall, 3.3 metres wide and weighs about 700 kilograms, and it is not an antique: the lantern is remade roughly every ten years by a lantern-maker in Kyoto, and the paper over your head is a recent replacement. Look at its base before you walk under — a carved wooden dragon curls around the bottom rim. The characters on the front read Kaminari-mon, thunder gate. On the back they read Furaijinmon, the gate of the wind and thunder gods, which is the building's real name and explains the two figures glaring out of the alcoves: Raijin, the thunder god, drumming on a ring of drums, and Fujin, the wind god, hauling a bag of gales over his shoulders. Between them they were asked to keep storms, floods and fire away from the temple behind you. Gods of weather, in a city of timber houses beside a river, is a sensible choice of guardian.

This gate has burned down at least four times, most recently in a fire that started in a neighbouring district in 1865, after which the entrance stood missing for ninety-five years. The gate in front of you went up in 1960, paid for by Konosuke Matsushita, the founder of the company we now call Panasonic, whose name survives on the lantern's metal base as a thank-you. So Tokyo's most photographed landmark is a twentieth-century gift from a tycoon who made electrical goods, standing where a military commander raised a gate in the tenth century. That is the city's whole method in one object.

Do two things before you move on. Walk around to the back and look at the two statues facing inward, with dragons' tails: these were given in 1978 to mark a temple anniversary and were carved by the sculptor Hirakushi Denchu at the age of 106. Then turn and look at the glass-and-wood tower diagonally across the junction, a stack of eight little houses designed by the architect Kengo Kuma in 2012. Its eighth floor is a free observation terrace with the best view in Asakusa — straight down onto this gate and the street beyond it — and almost nobody goes up.

Now walk through. The moment you are under the lantern you are on temple ground, and the rule for the next 250 metres is simple: the middle of the approach was traditionally the deity's, so keep to one side, and let the shops do their work on you.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. This is the outer gate of the temple grounds, not a ticketed sight — it is open day and night.
stops.openingHours: The gate itself is open around the clock and illuminated after dark, usually until about 23:00. The shopping street beyond it opens around 09:00 and closes between 17:00 and 18:00.
stops.accessibility: Level, paved and step-free through the gate, though the junction outside is busy and the kerbs at the crossing can be uneven. The gate passage itself is wide and flat.
stops.insiderTip: Walk round to the far side before you go through: the back of the giant lantern carries the gate's official name, Furaijinmon, and the two inward-facing statues with dragon tails were carved in 1978 by a sculptor who was 106 years old at the time.
stops.nextStopDirections: Pass under the lantern and walk north up the middle of the temple approach, keeping slightly to one side. Nakamise-dori is the shopping street directly in front of you — our next stop is about eighty metres along it.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daderot, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Nakamise-dori
stops.narration:
Look up the street: 250 metres of shops, two facing rows, 89 of them — 54 on the east side, 35 on the west — finishing at the temple's inner gate. This is not a shopping street that happened to grow beside a temple. It is a shopping street the temple created.

The deal that made it: after Tokugawa Ieyasu chose Edo as his base in 1590, pilgrims poured in, and the local men who cleaned and served the temple grounds were granted the right to keep shops along the approach, in the decades around 1688 to 1735. Clean for the temple, sell to the pilgrims. That is the origin of what is called the oldest shopping street in Japan, and the same bargain still runs it — the shopkeepers' association maintains the street to this day. The name Nakamise means "shops in the middle", between the outer gate behind you and the inner gate ahead. In the Edo period, the shops nearest the temple were the yakudana, tea houses that served pilgrims; the ones at this end were hiramise, selling toys, sweets and souvenirs, exactly as they do now.

What has changed is the packaging. An 1885 brick arcade was wrecked by the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923; its vermilion replacement burned in the air raids of March 1945; the shops you are walking between are post-war, and the metal shutters on every front were painted in 1992 with scenes of old Asakusa, under the direction of the painter Ikuo Hirayama. Come early enough and the whole street becomes a gallery with the doors down.

Asakusa sold entertainment before it sold souvenirs. Edo's licensed pleasure district, the Yoshiwara, was moved out here after a fire in 1657, the kabuki theatres followed, and in 1903 Japan's first purpose-built cinema opened a few streets west of where you are standing. Pilgrims, then partygoers, then cinemagoers: the same cash registers, different hats.

Now spend something, because that is the point. The local specialities are ningyo-yaki, small sponge cakes baked in doll-shaped irons and filled with an — a sweet paste of azuki red beans, the base of most Japanese sweets; kaminari-okoshi, a brittle of puffed rice and sugar named after the thunder god at the gate; age-manju, a bun that has been deep-fried; and senbei, grilled rice crackers sold in stacks. Prices are fixed and cheap — most snacks run a few hundred yen — and nobody haggles, though many stalls now take cards and phone payments. One rule is quietly enforced by disapproval rather than by signs: eating as you walk is frowned upon, so buy, then stop beside the shop to eat.

The street runs on daylight — open around 09:00, shut by 17:00 or 18:00, some shops taking a weekday off. The crowd is everything people warn you about, and it is true: by ten in the morning this lane is a slow-moving queue. At seven it is empty, the shutters are down, and the temple at the end is lit like a stage. That is the version worth waking up for.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Everything you buy is at shop prices — most snacks cost a few hundred yen; carry some coins and small notes.
stops.openingHours: Most shops open around 09:00 and close between 17:00 and 18:00, and some take a weekday off. The street itself is always open, and the painted shutters are worth seeing outside shop hours.
stops.accessibility: Level, paved and step-free for the full 250 metres, but narrow and extremely crowded from mid-morning; come early if you use a wheelchair, a pushchair or a stick.
stops.insiderTip: Before the shops open, walk the street and look at the shutters — the "Asakusa picture scroll" murals were painted on them in 1992 under the painter Ikuo Hirayama. Then buy kaminari-okoshi, the puffed-rice sweet named after the thunder god above the gate you just walked through.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue north to the end of the street: the big two-storey gate with three hanging lanterns is Hozomon, the temple's inner gate. Pass through it. The main hall opens up straight ahead, and the tall pagoda stands to your left — that courtyard is our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: AudaCity3371, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Senso-ji Main Hall & Five-Storey Pagoda
stops.narration:
You are standing in front of the oldest temple in Tokyo, dedicated to a statue almost nobody has ever seen. In 628, two brothers, fishermen named Hinokuma Hamanari and Hinokuma Takenari, pulled a small golden figure of Kannon out of the Sumida River in their net. They threw it back; it came back. The headman of their village, Haji no Nakatomo, enshrined it in his house, and in 645 a monk named Kaisho built a hall for it. That is the founding, and the figure is the same one still kept here, inside a shrine within the main hall, never put on display. Kannon is the bodhisattva of compassion — a being who has postponed its own final enlightenment in order to help everyone else reach theirs — and this particular statue is a hibutsu, a hidden Buddha, kept from every eye including, by tradition, the priests'. People have prayed to a statue no one can see for fourteen centuries.

What everyday worship looks like, since you are welcome to join: at the water pavilion outside, the chozuya, take one ladleful — rinse your left hand, then your right, then a little into your cupped hand to rinse your mouth, and tip the ladle upright so the last water runs down the handle for the next person. At the great bronze incense burner, the jokoro, waft the smoke toward whatever part of you needs mending — eyes, knees, lungs; the smoke is understood as healing. At the offering box, drop a coin, then stand with your palms together and bow. Do not clap: clapping is how you address a kami, the deity of a Shinto shrine, not a Buddha. And if you draw an omikuji, a paper fortune ranked from daikichi, great blessing, down to kyo, misfortune, keep it in your wallet or tie it to the rack beside the others; nobody minds either way.

Now the buildings, because the honesty matters. Everything around you is twentieth-century concrete wearing old clothes. The main hall you are facing was rebuilt between 1951 and 1958, with a lightweight titanium roof added in 2010; the gate behind you, Hozomon, was rebuilt in 1964 and is hung with enormous hand-woven straw sandals; the five-storey pagoda to your left was rebuilt in 1973 on the site of a pagoda first raised in 942. All of it burned on 10 March 1945, in the firebombing raid that destroyed this quarter of the city and killed around 100,000 people by most estimates. The temple's Edo-period halls had been national treasures. What stands here now is the city's decision, made in the ruins, that Asakusa would come back.

The pagoda is worth a long look. At just under 53 metres it is one of the tallest in Japan, and its five roofs stand for the five elements of Buddhist cosmology — earth, water, fire, wind and void. In its topmost store rests a relic of the Buddha's ashes, a gift from a temple in Sri Lanka in 1966. Pagodas descend from the Indian stupa, originally a burial mound for relics, which is why a Buddhist temple has one and a Shinto shrine never does. And inside, running up the centre, is a pillar that is not quite fixed to the floors around it: the shinbashira, the central mast that lets the tower rock and settle in an earthquake instead of cracking. Hold on to that idea. The tower at the end of this walk borrowed it.

Senso-ji was the Tokugawa shoguns' family temple, and their patronage made it the heart of Edo's faith and Edo's money. It still draws around thirty million visitors a year. The hall opens at about 06:00, or 06:30 from October to March; the courtyard never closes, and the buildings are lit until late. Dawn is when this place is unmistakably a temple rather than an attraction.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. There is no ticket for the grounds, the main hall or the pagoda exterior; amulets, paper fortunes, the treasure hall and the sutra copying desk charge separately.
stops.openingHours: The grounds are open at all hours. The main hall opens at about 06:00 (06:30 from October to March) and its doors close at 17:00. The halls are illuminated in the evening, usually until around 23:00.
stops.accessibility: Flat, wide, step-free courtyard with paved and gravel surfaces. The main hall has a ramp and a lift to the worship area. The pagoda interior is not open to visitors.
stops.insiderTip: Come back at dawn: the hall opens at 06:00 or 06:30, the incense is already burning and the courtyard is close to empty for an hour. Then walk the east edge of the compound to find Nitenmon, the 1618 wooden gate and one of only two buildings here to survive the 1945 firebombing.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the main hall, walk east across the courtyard and leave through the old wooden gate, Nitenmon, dated 1618. Immediately beyond it stands a large stone torii, the gateway of Asakusa Shrine — our next stop, about two hundred metres away.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Joli Rumi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Asakusa Shrine (Sanja-sama)
stops.narration:
Ten steps from a Buddhist temple and you are in a different religion. This is Asakusa Shrine, known to everyone as Sanja-sama, "the three shrines", and it is here to honour the three men of the story you just heard: the fishermen Hamanari and Takenari, who found the Kannon in the river, and Haji no Nakatomo, the village headman who enshrined it. Three ordinary people, made sacred. In Shinto they are kami — a word usually translated as gods or spirits, though it means something more like the sacred power present in a mountain, a tree, an ancestor or an exceptional person. Shrines are where people approach that power; this one approaches it through two fishermen and a landlord.

Look at the hall: dark timber, deep eaves, a roof carved and gilded, built in 1649 on the orders of the third Tokugawa shogun, Iemitsu, and designated an Important Cultural Property by the Japanese government in 1951. It and the Nitenmon gate you just passed through are the only two buildings on this whole temple-and-shrine ground to come through the firebombing of 1945. Everything else was made again in concrete. Run your eye over the unweathered grain of the pillars and you are looking at the only seventeenth-century carpentry left here.

The relationship between the shrine and the temple next door is a lesson in Japanese religion. Until 1868 they were one institution, part temple and part shrine, and the deity here was worshipped under a Buddhist name. Then the Meiji government, modernising and centralising the country, ordered the forcible separation of Shinto and Buddhism — a policy known as shinbutsu bunri, "the splitting of the gods and the Buddhas". Shrines across Japan were stripped of their Buddhist buildings and vocabulary; this one was renamed. The split is why you can now walk between the two in a minute, and it is a political act of the 1860s, not an ancient arrangement. Most Japanese today keep both halves anyway: married at a shrine, buried by a temple, and untroubled by the contradiction.

The shrine's public life is the Sanja Matsuri, held over three days around the third Friday to Sunday of May and one of the three great festivals of Tokyo, alongside the Kanda and Sanno festivals. What you would see: the ujiko, the people born into this parish, carrying mikoshi. A mikoshi is a portable shrine, a miniature of the building you are looking at, lacquered black and covered in gold leaf, with a long pole through it; inside it the kami is invited to travel. The three main mikoshi weigh about a tonne each and cost around ¥40 million to build, and around a hundred more, one for each neighbourhood association, take to the streets with them. Some two million people come to watch. The festival's punishing, wonderful climax is on the Sunday night, when the three big mikoshi are carried back into these grounds by firelight and cheering.

Two habits worth copying while you are here. Shrine etiquette is two bows, two claps, one bow — the opposite of the temple, where you keep your hands silent. And the amulets, omamori, and paper charms, ofuda, sold at the small office are not souvenirs: they are consecrated objects, replaced each year and returned to the shrine to be ritually burned rather than thrown away. The office keeps roughly 09:00 to 17:00, and weddings are held here most weekends — if you see a procession in traditional dress, admire it from a distance and do not photograph the people without asking. In cold, quiet February the shrine is mostly yours.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter and to pray. Amulets, charms and shrine ceremonies are charged separately — verify prices at the office.
stops.openingHours: The grounds are open at all hours. The shrine office for amulets and charms keeps roughly 09:00 to 17:00, and the hall may be closed to visitors during ceremonies and weddings.
stops.accessibility: Level gravel and stone courtyard with a couple of shallow steps up to the worship hall. A solid, firm surface that works for wheelchairs in dry weather.
stops.insiderTip: Check the hall against the concrete temple next door: this 1649 building and the 1618 Nitenmon gate are the only two survivors of the 1945 firebombing on this ground. In May the Sanja Matsuri fills the streets with about a hundred mikoshi — portable shrines — carried by parishioners.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the shrine's stone torii and walk south-east, following the streets downhill toward the river — about seven minutes on foot. The riverside strip along the bank is Sumida Park: turn north onto the promenade with the water on your right and follow the row of bare cherry trees to our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bernard Spragg. NZ from Christchurch, New Zealand, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sumida Park
stops.narration:
You are on the flat riverside strip that runs for about a kilometre between the Azuma Bridge behind you and the Sakura Bridge upstream, on both banks of the river: the Taito ward side under your feet, the Sumida ward side across the water. Tokyo has grander gardens, but none more public than this one, and the reason is a shogun's order.

The trees along this bank are cherry trees — sakura — and the story is that they were planted at the instruction of Tokugawa Yoshimune, the eighth shogun, who ruled from 1716 to 1745 and is remembered as the reformer of the shogunate's finances. Whatever his motive, the effect was to give ordinary townspeople the same pleasure that had been the court's and the samurai class's: hanami, flower viewing. Hanami is not a stroll. It is a picnic under the blossoms, ideally with a group, food and something to drink, sustained by the understanding that the flowers last a week or two and then fall. The blossoms were not always cherry. Japanese courtiers admired plum blossom first, wrote poems about it first, and the cherry only took over as the national flower later; the older taste lingers in the plum trees you still see flowering in February.

Two things to count. The city plants around 640 cherry trees on the Taito side and some 350 opposite, mostly the variety Somei-yoshino — a single cultivar, propagated by cuttings for centuries, which is why cherry blossom sweeps across the whole of Japan in nearly the same week. A few weeping cherries, shidarezakura, trail at the edges. And in spring the park stays open after dark for yozakura, night viewing, when the trees are lit from below. That is when this park becomes unmistakably modern as well as old: you eat, drink and look up at pink blossom with the Skytree standing floodlit on the far bank. In 1733, the same shogun Yoshimune, moved by a famine the year before, ordered a memorial festival on this river to comfort the dead — and fireworks formed part of it. That ceremony became the Sumida River Fireworks Festival, still held on the last Saturday of July, still one of the biggest in Japan, with around 20,000 shells and something close to a million people lining these banks. So this short, ordinary riverside park is where the city's public pleasures — blossoms, picnics, fireworks — were invented and are still held.

Now the honest February note. The cherry trees around you are bare sticks. Blossom here comes in late March and early April, and if you arrived expecting it you are two months early. What is out in this cold, dry month are camellias, tsubaki, with their thick glossy leaves and heavy red flowers, and the first plums. The compensation is the view, which is better in winter than in spring: air this clear shows the Skytree hard-edged across the water, the Asahi beer buildings' golden flame below it, and the temple roofs behind you. Faith, industry and broadcasting in a single glance — the whole walk in one frame.

The park is free and open at all hours; in blossom season a low-cost open cafe and boat landings run along this bank. Paths are flat and paved. When you are ready, turn back downstream along the promenade toward the pale steel bridge.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, open at all hours. In blossom season a riverside open cafe and boat trips operate along the bank at their own prices.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours, every day. Busiest in cherry-blossom season, late March to early April; quiet on cold winter mornings.
stops.accessibility: Flat, paved and gravel riverside paths, step-free, with benches along the promenade. Sensible shoes for the gravel stretches.
stops.insiderTip: In February the trees are bare — the blossom comes late March to early April. What you get instead is the clearest air of the year, which frames the Skytree and the Asahi flame across the river better than the pink weeks do.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn back south along the riverside promenade and walk downstream for seven minutes or so, until the path rises onto the pale steel bridge. Walk out onto the span and stop in the middle, where the whole river opens up. That is our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Arashiyama, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Azuma Bridge & the Sumida River
stops.narration:
Stand in the middle of the bridge and look both ways. This is the Sumida, the river that made the city you are standing in, and for two and a half centuries it was the main road of Edo — except that the traffic was on water.

The bridge under your feet was first built in 1774, when a group of townsmen obtained permission from the shogunate to put a crossing here. What makes that unusual is that the other Edo-period bridges over this river — Ryogoku, Eitai, Shin-Ohashi — were funded by the government. This one was a private-public partnership, three centuries early. The name means "east", after the road that ran east out of the city, and the elegant characters now used for it are an old poetic word for the eastern provinces. A fire, a flood and the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 each finished off a version of the bridge; the present steel span dates from 1931.

Now look at the water and imagine it as infrastructure. In the Edo period this river had a different name at every stretch — Asakusa-gawa here, Ryogoku-gawa downstream, Okawa near the bay — and it carried nearly everything the city consumed: rice, timber, sake, charcoal, salt and fish, unloaded at warehouses that lined these banks. It also carried away what the city produced, including human waste, collected in barrels and sold to farmers upriver as fertiliser, which is how a city with almost no livestock still fed its fields. Edo grew to around a million people by the early 1700s, probably the largest city on earth at the time, and it ate because of this river and the canals cut off it.

It was also dangerous. This channel is the old course of the Arakawa, a river with a violent temper, and in 1910 two typhoons in one season sent it over its banks and drowned much of eastern Tokyo. The answer was engineering on a national scale: a 22-kilometre floodway dug to take the Arakawa's bulk around the city instead of through it, begun in 1911 and finished in 1930, with a sluice gate upstream that still meters how much water is allowed into the Sumida. The quiet, tame, walkable river below you is a machine that took two decades and a disaster to build. It is tidal this far up, too — the level slides up and down with Tokyo Bay twice a day, which is why the bank looks different in the evening.

Then the river nearly died of success. By the 1960s this was an open sewer, the fish were gone, and the fireworks — held here since 1733 — were suspended from 1961 to 1977. Stricter rules on factory and household waste, dredging and fresh water piped in from other rivers brought it back; cormorants and herons fish here again, and the crowds came back with them.

What you see now is the old leisure river reborn. The roofed party boats with tatami floors, the yakatabune, still cruise these banks at night as they have for centuries. The water buses from the pier below you run down the Sumida to the bay, and one of them, a silver teardrop called Himiko, was designed by the manga artist Leiji Matsumoto, creator of Space Battleship Yamato. Upstream you can see the flat pedestrian Sakura Bridge and beyond it the Kototoi Bridge; downstream, the Asahi buildings and the Skytree, which line up for the photograph every visitor to this city eventually takes. Then cross to the far bank and go down to the water on the right, toward the golden flame.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The bridge and the riverside walks cost nothing; the yakatabune party boats and the water buses below charge their own fares.
stops.openingHours: The bridge and both riverbanks are open at all hours. Water-bus sailings run through the day — check the timetable at the pier before counting on one.
stops.accessibility: Pavements on both sides of the bridge with a shallow rise onto the span. Steps connect the approaches to the riverside terrace on the downstream side; the bridge crossing itself is smooth and step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Come back onto the downstream side of the bridge at dusk: the Asahi flame and the Skytree line up over the water, and when the wind drops the tower reflects in the Sumida. Look up and down the river for the two very different sights — old pleasure boats and a 634-metre broadcast mast.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross to the far side of the bridge and take the steps or the ramp down to the right-hand embankment, following the water downstream. The low black hall crowned with a golden sculpture is a two-minute walk along the embankment, beside the tall amber building — our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Kakidai, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Asahi Beer Hall & the Flamme d'Or
stops.narration:
Two buildings stand here, and the joke about one of them has been running since 1989. Start with what they actually are.

The tall amber tower is the headquarters of Asahi, one of Japan's big four brewers — Asahi means "morning sun". It was built as a centennial project, and it is not a rectangle: the golden mirrored glass up to the twentieth floor is meant to be the colour of freshly poured beer, and the white cladding on the top two floors is meant to be the head of foam, so the whole tower reads as an overflowing mug. The low black hall beside it, set on a granite base, is the Asahi Beer Hall, also called Super Dry Hall after the company's most famous beer, a crisp lager launched in 1987 that reset the Japanese market. It was designed by the French designer Philippe Starck and finished in 1989.

And on its roof sits the reason everyone photographs a brewery headquarters. The sculpture's official name is Flamme d'Or — French for Golden Flame. It is 44 metres long and weighs 360 tonnes, which is about as much as thirty buses. It is steel, it is hollow, and it was fabricated by shipbuilders using techniques borrowed from submarine construction, because a curved, welded, watertight shell that big is shipyard work rather than building work. It rests on a black granite pedestal shaped like the base of a torch. Asahi's own explanation is that it represents "Asahi's burning passion and drive toward a new century"; earlier versions of the line called it the burning heart of Asahi beer. The sculptor's other Tokyo building from the same years looks like a shed with growths. He was not a man who made quiet objects.

Now the nickname. In Japanese it is kin no unko — the golden poo — and the building is unko-biru, the poo building. It is not an insult so much as an observation about graphic convention: Japan draws droppings as exactly that soft upward swirl with a tapered tip, and Asahi built one, in gold, on a pedestal, at a scale visible from several bridges. The company has never adopted the joke, and has occasionally had to fight it. In late 2017 the sculpture vanished under sheeting, and social media celebrated the end of an eyesore until Asahi's customer service line had to explain that it was simply being repainted. There is also a widely repeated story that the flame was designed to stand upright and was rotated after someone pointed out the resemblance. Everyone in Tokyo tells it; nobody has documented it. Treat it as folklore — good folklore, the kind that sticks because the object really is that ambiguous.

Two practical notes. The beer hall and restaurant at the base pour the company's beer and serve food at normal Tokyo prices, and the headquarters tower has long kept a free cafe-bar on its twenty-second floor with a view back across the river — check whether it is open before you plan to climb. And when you have finished looking, turn east: the canal called the Kitajikken-gawa runs away from the Sumida here toward Oshiage, with a promenade beside it under the railway viaduct and past a small row of waterside shops called Tokyo Mizumachi. Follow the canal east for about a kilometre, a walk of roughly fifteen minutes, and the base of the tower slowly fills the sky in front of you.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk past and photograph — these are the company's working headquarters and beer hall. The beer hall and restaurant inside charge normal Tokyo prices; verify its opening hours before planning a meal.
stops.openingHours: The riverside plaza outside is open at all hours. The beer hall, restaurant and the tower's upper-floor cafe keep their own hours and occasionally close — check before going in.
stops.accessibility: Level, step-free riverside path and plaza beneath the buildings, with a gentle slope down from the bridge.
stops.insiderTip: Walk the upstream side for the composition everyone comes for: the golden flame in the foreground with the Skytree rising behind it, both reflecting in the Sumida when the water is calm. The nickname — kin no unko, the golden poo — is unofficial; the company calls it the Flamme d'Or, the golden flame.
stops.nextStopDirections: Follow the water east: the canal called the Kitajikken-gawa leaves the Sumida here and runs toward Oshiage, with a promenade alongside it under the railway viaduct and past the waterside row of shops at Tokyo Mizumachi. Keep the canal on your left and walk about a kilometre — fifteen minutes at an easy pace — until the tower's base fills the sky. If you would rather not walk it, the Tobu Skytree line runs one stop from Asakusa Station to Tokyo Skytree Station.

stops.name: Tokyo Skytree
stops.narration:
Look straight up until your neck complains. That is 634 metres of steel, the tallest tower in the world, and only two buildings on earth stand higher. The height is a rebus: 6 is mu, 3 is sa, 4 is shi — musashi, the old province that covered modern Tokyo, Saitama and part of Kanagawa. The name of the tower was chosen by public vote in 2008; the number was chosen to be remembered.

It exists for a reason you can test by looking at the television in your hotel room. Japan switched off analogue television on 24 July 2011. Tokyo Tower, 333 metres and built in 1958, served analogue perfectly well, but digital signals behave differently, and the city's newer skyscrapers began shadowing a mast that was no longer high enough. NHK and five commercial broadcasters needed a transmitter roughly twice as tall, and Tobu, a private railway company, offered its disused freight yard at Narihirabashi as the site and paid to build it — for broadcasting, and to regenerate a corner of the city its trains served. Construction ran from July 2008 to February 2012; it opened on 22 May 2012 and cost about ¥65 billion. It carries the region's digital television and FM radio, and it is designed to keep working as an emergency communications mast when everything else fails.

Now the part that ties this walk together. The tower's structure is a lattice of around 37,000 steel members over a reinforced concrete core, triangular at the base, and its profile uses two curves with Japanese names borrowed from sword-making: sori, the sweep of the blade, and mukuri, the flare where it meets the grip. The clever bit is that the concrete core is deliberately not rigidly tied to the steel frame above the base, so in an earthquake the core and the shell can move against each other and cancel out the sway. That central pillar has a name: the shinbashira — the same word used for the mast inside a five-storey pagoda — the one you stood beside at Senso-ji. A tenth-century Buddhist idea, retested at 634 metres. It was tested for real on 11 March 2011, when the Tohoku earthquake struck while the tower was half-built; it rode the shaking out undamaged.

Ride up: the Tembo Deck at 350 metres, with a glass floor section for the brave, then the Tembo Galleria at 450 metres, a sloping glass corridor that spirals to the tower's highest point at 451 metres — the upper deck needs the pricier ticket. On a clear day the view reaches about 70 kilometres. February is the month to do this: the winter air over the Kanto plain is the clearest of the year, and to the west, on a good morning or late afternoon, you get Mount Fuji — 3,776 metres, the country's highest mountain and the object of a whole mountain-worship tradition, snow-capped and unbothered by the city at its feet.

Timing matters here. Online advance tickets start at around ¥1,800 for the 350-metre deck and around ¥3,000 for the deck plus the 450-metre galleria; buying at the counter on the day adds a ¥500 service fee per ticket, so book a timed slot — it is cheaper and it skips the queue. Hours shift by date, running roughly 09:00 or 10:00 until 21:00 or 22:00, with last admission about an hour before closing.

If you would rather stay at ground level, the tower's base is Tokyo Solamachi, a mall of around 300 shops and restaurants, and on its fifth and sixth floors sits the Sumida Aquarium: an indoor pool with about fifty Magellanic penguins, a jellyfish basin called the Big Schale holding roughly 500 jellyfish, and a gallery of goldfish — the fish the old shitamachi bred in tubs behind its houses. Adult tickets are around ¥2,700, and its hours shift by date, so verify at the door.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Online advance tickets start at around ¥1,800 for the 350-metre Tembo Deck and around ¥3,000 for the deck plus the 450-metre Tembo Galleria; buying on the day at the counter adds a ¥500 service fee per ticket. Prices move and vary by date — verify on the day. The Sumida Aquarium in the base charges separately, around ¥2,700 for adults.
stops.openingHours: Open daily with seasonal hours — roughly 09:00 or 10:00 until 21:00 or 22:00, and last admission about an hour before closing. The day's timetable changes with holidays, so check it before you travel. The shopping mall and the area around the base are open and free at all hours.
stops.accessibility: Fully accessible and step-free: lifts to both observation decks, accessible toilets, wheelchairs available on request, and barrier-free routes from Tokyo Skytree and Oshiage stations. The Tembo Galleria's sloped corridor has a glass-floor section that can be skirted if you prefer to avoid it.
stops.insiderTip: February gives the clearest air of the year and the best chance of Mount Fuji, visible to the west on clear mornings and late afternoons. Book a timed ticket online — it starts lower than the counter price and skips the day's queue. The tower's lighting changes colour by theme each night; the schedule is posted in the entrance hall.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. If there is any daylight left, go up and come down after dark — the deck at dusk is the reason to finish here. If you would rather stay at ground level, Tokyo Solamachi fills the base with shops and food halls, and the Sumida Aquarium is on the fifth and sixth floors. To get back, Oshiage and Tokyo Skytree stations are right at the tower's foot: the Tobu line runs one stop to Asakusa, or you can walk back across the Azuma Bridge in the dark, when the tower and the golden flame stand in the water together. From Asakusa, the Ginza, Toei Asakusa and Tsukuba Express lines go back into the centre.
